title: No Top to the Mountain
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains the craft of writing an "Everest Statement" -- a classroom mission statement whose definition of success is a mountain with no top, so every student, regardless of starting point, always has room to grow. He shares his own world-history Everest Statement and a Latin teacher's example, highlighting verbs like "becoming" and "progressing" that keep the goal aspirational rather than fixed. He diagnoses a widespread, often invisible motivation problem: students who define success narrowly as "getting a good grade" or "passing" lose their reason to keep working once that bar is cleared, breeding complacency and disengagement -- a failure of the Efficacy belief. This is why "Define Success: Wisely, Early, and Often" survived his cut from 55 candidate strategies down to the 10 in The Will to Learn. The piece closes by reframing mastery itself as a mountain with no summit, one that only grows more beautiful the further a student climbs.
points: An effective Everest Statement deliberately describes a "mountain with no real top," so every student -- high-achieving or struggling -- always has authentic room left to grow.

Narrow definitions of success ("good grades," "passing") quietly sabotage motivation: once a student secures that bar, the Efficacy belief has nothing left to drive it, producing complacency and disengagement.

Stuart cut his original 55-strategy manuscript down to 10 for The Will to Learn, and "Define Success: Wisely, Early, and Often" survived because it solves a fundamental, often-invisible motivation problem present in every classroom.
Word choice matters: verbs like "becoming" and "progressing" in an Everest Statement keep success framed as movement rather than arrival, making the statement relevant to every student in the room.
quotes: A widespread (and often invisible!) obstacle to secondary student motivation is that their definitions of success are too narrow. They define success as "getting good grades" or "passing the class.

Once I've got my good grade secured or I'm not at risk of failing, I have no reason to keep working. I no longer believe that I can succeed — the Efficacy belief, pp. 167-218 in The Will to Learn — because now, I have succeeded.
Once I've arrived at success, I won't care as much. I've arrived. It's a classic recipe for complacency, boredom, and disengagement.
Those words becoming and progressing are so important. They emphasize movement toward mastery, building toward strength — and by doing that, they become relevant to every student in the class.

So make sure your Everest Statement describes success as a mountain that actually has no end. Because that's what growing toward mastery is: a journey up a mountain with no end. And the further you climb that mountain of mastery, the more and more beautiful it gets.
